title: The Mool Mantar, sounded
hook: Ik Onkar, Satnam, Karta Purakh, Nirbhau, Nirvair, Akal Murat, Ajuni, Saibhang, Gur Prasad

segments.voice: Yesterday, Japji Sahib. Your line was listen before you understand. Did Japji play once, all the way through, and did one sound stay with you? Day one hundred fifty-nine.

Every community has a line people know by heart. The words that come out without thinking, at a wedding, a funeral, a bedside. Sikhs have one that comes before everything else. It opens the Guru Granth Sahib. It opens Japji. A short form of it stands at the head of hymns all through the scripture. It's called the Mool Mantar, the root verse. Today we don't explain it. We just learn how it sounds.
screen: `A LINE EVERYONE KNOWS.` → `IT OPENS THE WHOLE GRANTH.` → `TODAY, ONLY THE SOUND.`

segments.voice: Mool means root. Mantar is a verse to be repeated. The root verse. Here it is, slowly, in its pieces. Ik Onkar. Ik, like ick; Onkar, ong-KAAR. Sat Naam. Sat, rhyming with but; naam, like calm with an n. Kartaa Purakh. KAR-taa, PUR-akh. Nirbhau. nir-BHOW, like now, with a breath on the b. Nirvair. nir-VAIR, like air. Akaal Moorat. a-KAAL, MOO-rat. Ajoonee. a-JOO-nee. Saibhang. say-BHUNG. Gur Prasaad. gur pra-SAAD. That's the whole thing: fourteen short words, the way we've spaced them here. Said slowly, it takes less than half a minute. You met some of their meanings back on days four and five, and we'll keep meeting them all through Japji: one; truth is the name; the maker; without fear; without hate; beyond time; unborn; self-existent; known by the Guru's grace. Now notice the sound itself. It moves in short beats, two and three syllables at a time, easy to breathe with. Its first sound is a number: ik, one. Its middle is a run of nirs and a's, nirbhau, nirvair, akaal, ajoonee, each one saying what the One is not: not afraid, not hating, not bound by time, not born. And the last two words, gur prasaad, turn the whole verse into a gift: this isn't something you figure out, it's something given. Sikhs differ a little on where the Mool Mantar ends. Some end it at gur prasaad. Others carry on through the next lines, to Naanak hosee bhee sach. Either way, every word of it is said each morning at the start of Japji.
screen: `MOOL — ROOT. MANTAR — VERSE.` · `SHORT BEATS, EASY TO BREATHE.` · `IT STARTS WITH A NUMBER.` · `GUR PRASAAD — A GIFT.` · then, large: `THE MOOL MANTAR.`

segments.voice: Now it's yours. Sit up, breathe in, and say it slowly, out loud if you can, in a whisper if you can't. Ik Onkar. Sat Naam. Kartaa Purakh. Nirbhau. Nirvair. Akaal Moorat. Ajoonee. Saibhang. Gur Prasaad. Take a breath between each piece. Then say it once more, a little smoother. Don't worry about every vowel; say what you heard. If you pray, it's already a prayer. If you're learning, it's a sound worth knowing by heart. The bell holds the time.
screen: `ੴ ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁ ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁ ਨਿਰਭਉ ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿ ਅਜੂਨੀ ਸੈਭੰ ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ`

segments.voice: Mool Mantar. The root verse that opens the Guru Granth Sahib, from Ik Onkar to Gur Prasaad.
Your line: sound it out. Say the Mool Mantar once more before you sleep tonight, slowly, from Ik Onkar to Gur Prasaad. Day one hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite the Mool Mantar at the start of Japji each morning and at many other moments; a short form, Ik Onkar Satgur Prasad, stands at the head of hymns throughout the Guru Granth Sahib.

match.prompt: match the sound to its sense.

myth: the Mool Mantar is a long passage
it's fourteen short words, as we spaced them, and takes less than half a minute to say slowly.
its very first sound is a number
every Sikh ends it at exactly the same word
some end at gur prasaad; others carry on to Naanak hosee bhee sach.

fork.setup: the Mool Mantar is a short verse. what is its very first sound?
fork.reveal: ik, one. the whole Guru Granth Sahib begins with a number.

original.script: ੴ ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁ ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁ ਨਿਰਭਉ ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿ ਅਜੂਨੀ ਸੈਭੰ ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ
original.say: ik ong-KAAR, sat NAAM, KAR-taa PUR-akh, nir-BHOW, nir-VAIR, a-KAAL MOO-rat, a-JOO-nee, say-BHUNG, gur pra-SAAD
original.note: Gurmukhi: the Mool Mantar, the root verse, Ang 1.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of names for God.
what it means: the root verse: one, truth, maker, without fear or hate, beyond time, unborn, self-existent, given by grace.
what a scholar hears: the little vowel marks at the end of words like naam and purakh carry grammar and are mostly left silent in recitation.

sources.ref: Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 1, the Japji (preamble)

notes: Pronunciation guides are approximate for English speakers; a Keeper or gyani should check them, especially Onkar and Saibhang.
Where the Mool Mantar ends (at gur prasaad, or through 'hosi bhi sach') is a known difference of view; confirm phrasing.
Short forms heading hymns (Ik Onkar Satgur Prasad): confirm.
Final aunkar/sihari usually unvoiced in recitation: confirm wording for learners.

Review (2026-10-01): 'about a dozen words' corrected to fourteen as spaced in the script; 'fifteen seconds' and 'many Sikh children' claims removed; 'many end it at gur prasaad' made neutral ('some... others'); 'half-heard their outline' (garbled) now points to days 4 and 5.
